rationale: Coordinate grids compare adult shapes; they do not show that organisms generally grow along the streamlines of an interspecific orthogonal map. Departures from orthogonality are not, in general, evidence that the tissue failed to be homogeneous and isotropic.

Local mechanical constraints do shape some tubes, vesicles, and fruits, but those organs usually form by patterned proliferation, active bending, and differentiation rather than by uniform isotropic expansion held in by a few trammels.

A smooth deformation can approximate the outline change from a porcupinefish to an ocean sunfish, but it does not account for all external differences, and the classic figure was fitted by eye rather than derived as a unique integral map that leaves the head fixed.

Living crocodylians share a conservative skull that deformations can summarize in part, but one simple transformation does not recover every bone and opening. The short, specialized skull of Notosuchus is not a bone-for-bone coordinate image of Crocodylus.

Horse skulls show a real trend toward a longer face and taller cheek teeth, so some fossils resemble blends of early and late forms. The match is not close in detail, and Protohippus is not a precise station on one transformation from Hyracotherium to Equus.
Parahippus lies near the origin of the grazing horses that lead toward Equus, not clearly off that line. A poor fit to a straight morphometric interpolation is not evidence of phylogenetic exclusion.
Perissodactyls group with other ungulates among laurasiatherians, while rabbits group with rodents. Similar skull flexure is convergence and does not indicate closer relationship.

Human, chimpanzee, and baboon skulls differ largely by an integrated shift in facial projection and braincase size that one deformation can summarize. The change is only roughly logarithmic, and the face, cranial base, and vault also vary partly independently.
A fossil monkey, Homo erectus, Neanderthals, and modern humans do not form one ancestor-descendant sequence. Hominoid cranial evolution is branching rather than a single transformation series.

Flattened fishes are often deeper and thinner than round-bodied fishes, which keeps volume from changing as much as the linear dimensions, and similar length-weight coefficients for plaice and haddock are plausible. A strict twofold tradeoff is only a rough tendency, and those two species are not close relatives.
Measurement of shape, growth, and mechanical constraint is now basic to morphology and is required to explain form, alongside descriptive anatomy.
A few regular structures, notably the honeycomb, are functionally efficient, but mathematical regularity does not generally coincide with usefulness across natural forms.
Organisms are ordinary matter, and no vital exemption from physical law is known. Living processes are constrained by the same physics as non-living ones.

Theories may be stated as discrete computational rules as well as differential equations. Both are legitimate when they match the phenomena, so traditional equations are not the only admissible form of a definite rule.

Surveys of small programs show that many simple rules produce nesting, apparent randomness, or persistent localized structures. Some of the smallest, including a computation-universal elementary cellular automaton, reach as high a computational level as any familiar discrete system.

Simple rules can generate complex patterns, and no supernatural source is required. The complexity of real physical and biological systems is not in general explained by those systems being typical simple programs.

Equations describe many complex phenomena, including fluids, quantum systems, and populations, and natural selection explains a large body of adaptive complexity. Program-based descriptions add a tool; they are not forced by a general failure of equations.

Across cellular automata, machines, and rewriting systems, the same coarse behaviors recur despite different rule formats. That supports limited generalities of behavior, while the further claim that they govern systems throughout nature is an extrapolation.

Statistical mechanics already derives macroscopic irreversibility from typical microscopic states. Recasting that argument in terms of simple programs has not become the accepted resolution of the second law.
A computational substrate for physics is an open possibility, but simple programs have not yielded an accepted theory from which space, time, and quantum mechanics emerge.
An elementary cellular automaton whose rule fits in one sentence, and some very small Turing machines, are capable of arbitrary computation.
Universality is easier to reach in abstract rule systems than earlier informal expectations suggested. That does not show that computationally universal behavior is common in nature.
Behavior that is not obvious comes in different strengths, from statistical disorder to universal computation. Systems that merely look complicated are not all computationally equivalent.
Some patterns are hard to compress, but their apparent complexity is not explained by an equivalence between human perception and the process being observed.

Many discrete systems have no known shortcut and must be iterated step by step. Other complex systems still admit reduced descriptions, so irreducibility is common rather than the normal fate of everything that is not simple.
Computational unpredictability limits forecasting of a deterministic system. It does not establish that humans have free will in the sense at issue in that debate.
A universal simple program can emulate any computable process in principle. Human intelligence is not matched in organization or performance by typical simple programs or by ordinary natural systems.

Simple rule systems can encode arbitrary computation, so many questions about them are unprovable in any fixed formal theory. Those limits reach beyond the arithmetic settings in which incompleteness was first shown.

Simple programs and reaction-diffusion models reproduce some pigmentation and branching patterns. The mapping from genomes to anatomy runs through specific regulatory and physical mechanisms, not generic program complexity.

Very small rule sets can be computationally universal, so a sophisticated task need not begin from a complicated primitive rule. Making such rules into reliable atomic-scale devices is a separate and largely unfulfilled engineering claim.

Chaotic maps produce irregular orbits from compactly described initial values. Sensitive dependence amplifies differences; it does not merely display complexity already stored in a simple initial condition.

Natural selection often accumulates adaptive complexity and only sometimes simplifies lineages. The bulk of conspicuous biological complexity is not attributed to the generic behavior of simple programs.

The elementary rule that colors a cell when exactly one neighbor is black is the exclusive-or of those neighbors and generates Pascal's triangle modulo two, a field of strictly self-similar triangles.
From a single black cell, elementary rule 30 produces a persistently irregular pattern rather than a periodic or nested one.
Short deterministic rules started from simple states, including cellular automata and iterated maps, routinely generate behavior with no simple closed form.
Emergence from simple rules contributes to some pattern formation. Most complexity in nature is accounted for by specific physical dynamics and, in living systems, by selection and history.

The center column of rule 30 shows no short period over prefixes of a million steps and passes standard statistical tests of randomness. It remains a deterministic sequence, so agreement with perfect randomness is empirical rather than proved.

Rule 110 mixes a regular background with persistent localized structures whose collisions make even average densities depend on a long interaction history, so those averages are harder to predict than for a noisy rule such as rule 30.

Because rule 110 is computationally universal, many questions about the fate of its localized structures have no general shortcut. For particular initial data, direct iteration is the method that actually decides them.

Iteration of rule 110 from one black cell leaves a single surviving structure that interacts with the periodic background from the left and repeats every 240 steps after a transient of about 2780 steps.
A single cellular-automaton rule supports quiescent backgrounds, moving localized structures, and collisions. Different arrangements of cell states, not different rules, produce those behaviors.
Engineering practice does favor systems whose behavior can be foreseen, and nature is not bound by that filter. It does not follow that complex organization generally lacks a complex specification.
A few natural patterns resemble the output of very small rules. Systems with the specific character of rule 30 or rule 110 have not been shown to be very common in nature.

Historical ornament is dominated by repeats and occasional hierarchical motifs. Patterns with the irregular complexity of simple cellular automata such as rule 30 do not appear as a traditional design type.
Computer enumeration and simulation have produced precise discoveries that are not merely numerical consequences of equations chosen in advance.
Systematic search can reveal unexpected phenomena, but theory, chance observation, and hypothesis-driven tests have also done so. It is not the only way.

Large surveys of rule space became practical only with later computers, which partly explains the timing of that work. Complicated behavior of simple systems was already visible earlier in hand exploration, the Game of Life, and chaotic maps.

Nontrivial properties of programs are undecidable in general, and ordinary programming confirms that short rules often have no transparent summary. Cellular-automaton rules show the same gap between a simple definition and its space-time behavior.

Primes have a short definition, and their gaps behave in many ways like a random set of the appropriate density. Number theory has also proved substantial regularities, so the distribution was not simply neglected in favor of order.
Pi is computed by short algorithms, and long prefixes of its digits pass ordinary tests of statistical randomness, although it is still unproved that the digits are normal.
Irregular output from short rules was already recognized in prime gaps, the digits of pi, chaotic maps, and the Game of Life before it was presented as a previously unnoticed basic phenomenon.

Enumerations of cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tags, and register machines produce the same coarse catalog: decay or constancy, periodicity, nesting, apparent randomness, and interacting localized structures.

Runs of all 256 elementary rules from one black cell split into a majority whose patterns stay bounded and about a third that grow, with only a modest fraction more elaborate than repetition. The stated fractions match that exhaustive classification.

Within those 256 rules, a small set looks random and falls into a few visual families, and a few dozen look nested and likewise reduce to a handful of distinct forms. The counts of 10 and 24 are the standard result of that classification, which has a modest subjective boundary.

Elementary two-color rules already produce randomness and localized structures, including universal computation. Adding colors or larger neighborhoods mostly repeats those kinds of behavior rather than creating a higher grade.

There are 2187 three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic rules, and exhaustive surveys find about 85 percent eventually regular, with the rest including noisy rules and rules with interacting localized structures.
The 65536 two-color mobile automata that rewrite only the active cell stay within repetition and nesting. More complex behavior appears only if neighbors can also change, and then only rarely.

In generalized mobile automata, disordered or particle-like evolution is seen almost only when many cells are active at once. That association fits the higher frequency of complexity in fully parallel cellular automata.

There are 4096 two-state two-color Turing machines and about three million three-state two-color machines, and blank-tape surveys find only patterns that settle into repetition or nesting. Long transients leave a residual chance that a few were under-classified.

With four head states, two-color Turing machines first show persistently irregular behavior, in roughly five rules per million, and further states raise that rate only slightly without new kinds of behavior.

A substitution that rewrites each element from its own color alone is an iterated morphism and builds a hierarchical self-similar pattern. Behavior beyond nesting requires the rule to depend on at least one neighbor.

Two-color neighbor-dependent substitutions that can delete elements and grow slowly stay repetitive in these enumerations. Allowing three or four colors readily yields noisy patterns comparable to cellular automata.

Sequential search-and-replace is enough for complex and even universal rewriting. With three replacements, random samples contain a small fraction, on the order of one in ten thousand, whose evolution looks irregular.

A tag system that deletes one element and appends a block determined by it is only a slowed morphism, so its patterns stay repetitive or nested. Deleting two elements per step is the classical tag process and can be highly complicated.
Simple cyclic tag systems, which can embed complex computation, often grow at a steady average rate while fluctuations about that trend look irregular.

Exhaustive search of two-register increment and decrement-jump programs finds only repetition up to four instructions, nesting in two programs of length five, nothing substantially richer through length seven, and complex behavior in 126 of the 11,019,960,576 programs of length eight.
Small register machines idealize short imperative programs, and sampling millions of short programs in low-level languages likewise turns up occasional irregular, random-looking runs.
Repeated application of a single combinator-like rewrite to nested expressions yields both stabilizing cases and cases whose growth is irregular and apparently random.

Complex behavior from simple rules persists in machines, tag systems, and symbolic rewriting, after the rigid lattice and synchronous update of cellular automata are removed. It is not an artifact of that one formalism.

In each of these families, repetition and nesting appear at very small rule size, and irregular or localized-structure behavior appears only slightly beyond that. The threshold for complexity is low wherever it has been surveyed.

Repetition, nesting, apparent randomness, and localized structures dominate large surveys of discrete systems, and which of them appears depends only weakly on syntactic details of the rules. Extension to an arbitrary vast range of systems is less secure.

Some physical universality classes allow coarse predictions without full microscopic detail. It is not established that the important features of natural systems are usually those already seen in the simplest programs.
Running an exactly specified program can reveal behavior the experimenter did not anticipate, and the observed run is as definite as a theorem about that rule and initial state.

Beginning with the smallest system that could show a phenomenon is often productive, because small rules already generate complexity. It is not always true that a simpler system would have sufficed, and the claim about the most common mistake is a judgment about practice.

Very short arithmetic iterations, including chaotic maps and the Collatz map, produce orbits whose structure is highly complicated and is found by direct computation rather than by a closed-form analysis.
